 Trump greeted at airport by Xi in extremely rare move ahead of meeting with Putin. Catch up
 By Catherine Nicholls 
 President Trump arrives in Shenzhen, China 
 Reuters 
 US President Donald Trump is now in Shenzhen, China, where he was greeted at the airport by Chinese leader Xi Jinping, a first for Xi in his current role.
 Historically, it is extremely rare for China’s top leader to personally welcome foreign leaders upon their arrivals.
 Trump is expected to take part in an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) banquet this evening, then several significant meetings tomorrow. 
 Here’s the latest: 
 Upon his arrival in China, Trump was greeted by enthusiastic spectators, a military flyover, an honor guard, and Xi. The Chinese leader said he met Trump at the airport to reciprocate after Trump personally greeted Xi when he arrived at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland earlier this year.
 Before this, Trump had a short stop in Manila, the Philippines. He touted a potential nuclear energy deal with the Philippines as he sat down with his counterpart Ferdinand Marcos Jr, and said that he was not worried about tensions between Manila and Beijing over the South China Sea.
 Meanwhile, during a meeting at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, the authoritarian leaders of Russia and China touted the stability of their relationship and its benefit to the world order.
 Russian President Vladimir Putin said he expects “considerable potential benefits” from his scheduled meeting with Trump and Xi tomorrow, Russian state media TASS reported.
 CNN’s Sylvie Zhuang, Kathleen Magramo and Lex Harvey contributed to this reporting.

 Trump to see why US efforts won't stop China's rise as tech behemoth
 Analysis by Simone McCarthy in Beijing
 The skyline in Shenzhen, China, is lit up for the upcoming APEC Summit on November 16, 2026. 
 Kevin Frayer/Getty Images 
 For Xi Jinping, a summit in the high-tech hub of Shenzhen this week is an opportune moment to showcase a vision of China’s unrelenting rise.
 Xi is hosting business moguls and world leaders for an annual regional economic summit, where he’ll sit down to sideline talks with US President Donald Trump and hold a three-way meeting with Trump and Russia’s Vladimir Putin, a first-ever trilateral for the nuclear-armed powers.
 And for his backdrop, Xi has chosen a host city that’s synonymous with China’s rapid transformation into a high-tech powerhouse — and its resilience in the face of US tech and trade frictions.
 A sprawling metropolis of 18 million, Shenzhen is home to a who’s-who of Chinese tech titans: hardware giant Huawei, dronemaker DJI and the Tesla-beating electric vehicle seller BYD — all companies that have thrived despite US import bans or blacklists.
 Once known as the capital of luxury knockoffs and cheap electronics, today the city’s high-tech products have helped propel China’s export juggernaut to a record $1 trillion trade surplus already this year.
 Visiting VIPs who step out onto Shenzhen’s streets this week will find traffic that moves to the whir of homegrown electric vehicles and novelty kiosks where robots serve up coffee. Self-driving taxis ferry passengers and drones deliver take-out in some areas. Surveillance cameras are ubiquitous.
 The high-tech vision may make for a sharp contrast to the US , where news this week has been dominated by a series of systems outages and a revelation that up until a few months ago the country’s aviation administration was still using floppy disks.

 After stopping in the Philippines, Trump is now in China. Here's what's on his schedule
 By Catherine Nicholls 
 US President Donald Trump arrives at his hotel in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday. 
 Pedro Pardo/AFP/Getty Images 
 US President Donald Trump is now in Shenzhen, China, after spending part of the day in Manila, the capital of the Philippines, during his ongoing Asia tour.
 Here’s a look at his remaining schedule: 
 Wednesday
 Trump was greeted at the airport in Shenzhen by Chinese leader Xi Jinping, who has never before gone to the airport to receive a visiting US president while in his current position.
 In a Xinhua news agency readout of Xi’s remarks to Trump, the Chinese leader said he was reciprocating after Trump met him at the airport when he visited the US earlier this year.
 At his hotel, Trump is set to hold meetings with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum, according to the White House press pool.
 The president is also expected to take part in a photo alongside Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders, which will be followed by a banquet.
 Thursday
 Tomorrow, Trump is expected to take part in an APEC conference session.
 He will then meet with Xi.
 Later in the day, he is also scheduled to take part in a meeting with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin. 
 Following this, Trump is scheduled to travel back to the White House.

 Trump greeted by fighter jets, an honor guard — and a warm embrace with Xi Jinping
 By Sylvie Zhuang 
 US President Donald Trump walks alongside Chinese President Xi Jinping as he arrives at Shenzhen Airport to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Leaders Summit in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday. 
 Carlos Barria/Reuters 
 Arriving in China for his second visit this year, Trump was greeted by enthusiastic spectators, a military flyover, an honor guard – and an embrace from Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
 When Trump exited Air Force One, he was greeted by rows of young women and men wearing pink and baby blue who were holding flowers and shouting “Welcome!”
 Xi and Trump embraced each other at the bottom of the steps. A girl handed Trump a bouquet of flowers, and then the US president shook hands with top communist party leaders one by one.
 Chinese President Xi Jinping welcomes US President Donald Trump. 
 Carlos Barria/Reuters 
 Trump is presented by flowers upon arrival. 
 Mark Schiefelbein/AP 
 A People’s Liberation Army (PLA) honor guard was present and five military jets flew over the airport, leaving pink, blue and yellow smoke trails in the sky.
 In a Xinhua readout of Xi’s remarks to Trump, the Chinese leader remembered how the US president and his wife made a “special trip to the airport to greet me, and a grand welcome ceremony was held,” referring to his trip to the US earlier this year.
 Trump greets people as Xi looks on. 
 Carlos Barria/Reuters 
 Trump and Xi are all smiles as they walk the red carpet. 
 Carlos Barria/Reuters 
 “China is a nation of courtesy, with a tradition of reciprocity,” the readout quoted Xi as saying.
 “I welcome you to visit China again, and I look forward to exchanging in-depth views with you on major issues concerning China-US. relations, Asia-Pacific cooperation, and the global landscape, so as to advance a constructive and stable strategic relationship between China and the United States based on respect, fairness, and reciprocity,” said Xi.
 Trump and Xi Jinping head for the motorcade.

 Why Xi may not meet Japan’s leader in China
 By Jessie Yeung 
 Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae speaks during the 81st United Nations General Assembly at the United Nations Headquarters in New York, on September 22. 
 Leonardo Munoz/AFP/Getty Images 
 Last October, Chinese leader Xi Jinping sat down for a meeting with Japan’s newly elected prime minister Sanae Takaichi. The two countries should be “partners, not threats” to each other, Xi told her.
 One year later, that hopeful statement has long been forgotten. China-Japan relations remain strained – with no sign the two leaders will meet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit this week.
 Their spat began just weeks after that first meeting when Takaichi suggested Japan could respond militarily if China were to move to take control of self-ruled Taiwan by force. China’s Communist Party claims Taiwan as its own territory, despite never having controlled it.
 Taiwan is one of China’s red lines – and Beijing was furious that Takaichi crossed it. Since then, China has put economic pressure on Japan, warning its citizens not to travel there; nationalist and anti-Japanese fervor spread on Chinese social media; and dozens of Japanese performers canceled performances in China, even if they didn’t cite the diplomatic row as a reason.
 When asked whether Xi would meet with Takaichi at APEC, a Chinese Foreign Affairs Ministry spokesperson gave a terse response.
 “As to China-Japan relations, we have made clear our position more than once.”
 That position is evident in a quick glance through the ministry’s briefings this past year.
 In November, it warned Japan: “Stop crossing the line and playing with fire.” In December: “We once again urge the Japanese side to reflect on and correct its wrongdoings.” Then in March: “Time for Japan to stop going further down the wrong path.”
 The countries have a long history of animosity. In the early 20th century, Japan’s Imperial Army invaded China and committed war crimes – including the Nanjing massacre . Japan has repeatedly apologized for the atrocities, but they remain a sharp pain point.

 China's leader Xi doesn't go the airport to meet US presidents. He just did for Trump
 By Sylvie Zhuang 
 President Trump arrives in Shenzhen, China 
 Reuters 
 During his time in the top job, Chinese leader Xi Jinping has never gone to the airport to receive a visiting US president.
 In protocol-obsessed China, Xi’s presence on the red carpet in Shenzhen highlights the importance China attaches to its bilateral relationship with the US.
 US President Donald Trump is greeted by Chinese leader Xi Jinping at Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport on November 18. 
 Win McNamee/Getty Images 
 Earlier this year, Trump personally greeted Xi when he arrived by plane at Joint Base Andrews.
 According to China’s diplomatic protocol in recent years, the head of state generally doesn’t go to the airport to greet guests.
 When Russia’s President Vladimir Putin arrived in Shenzhen earlier today, he was met by Xi’s powerful chief of staff Cai Qi – itself an unusually high level of protocol.
 Xi did greet then-US President Barack Obama at the airport in 2009, but he was China’s vice-president at the time.

 Trump is the first sitting US president to visit China’s "miracle city"
 By Sylvie Zhuang 
 The skyline is lit up for the upcoming APEC Summit on November 16 in Shenzhen, China. China will host the APEC Economic Leaders Summit on November 18-19. 
 Kevin Frayer/Getty Images 
 Donald Trump will become the first sitting US president to land in Shenzhen when he arrives for an APEC summit where Chinese leader Xi Jinping will show off the urban microcosm of his nation’s modern story: high-level planning, roaring technological advancement, and rapid wealth creation.
 There, Trump will find China’s answer to Silicon Valley; a city that’s home to tech entrepreneurs, food-delivering drones and the world’s fastest supercomputer.
 It’s a city that launched many of the tech advances that have put Trump and Xi on a collision course over access to raw materials, advanced chips, and lucrative markets.
 If you chat with any of Shenzhen’s 18 million people, they will proudly tell you it is a “miracle city.” Built out of mangrove wetlands over just four decades, the gleaming city boasts more skyscrapers than New York City and roughly three times more than Chicago, according to the Council on Vertical Urbanism.
 In the 80s, China’s then-leader Deng Xiaoping used the town, a stone’s throw from Hong Kong, to stage an experiment in free-market economics to attract foreign capital.
 Now, companies founded in Shenzhen are some of the best-known in the world: Huawei is one of the world’s biggest tech conglomerates, BYD overtook Elon Musk’s Tesla to become the world’s biggest seller of electric vehicles last year, Tencent owns social media giant WeChat and DJI is the world’s largest drone maker.

 In China, who greets you at the airport matters
 By Sylvie Zhuang in Hong Kong
 In China, who greets you at the airport and their rank in the communist party system is closely watched for clues to Beijing’s attitude towards the guest. A lower-level official might convey distance when Beijing is displeased; someone senior could signal respect and a willingness to build a closer bond.
 That was on show earlier on Wednesday.
 When Russian president Putin landed in Shenzhen for the APEC summit, he was greeted by Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s right-hand man, Cai Qi. Cai is the Chinese leader’s chief of staff and is considered by analysts as one the most powerful figures in the party system.
 Cai controls Xi’s schedule and security, meaning he is in charge of who gets to meet Xi and what information reaches the Chinese leader. He accompanies Xi on almost all of his trips and always sits on the right side of him.
 Ruply Russian Pool via Reuters 
 Cai has previously been sent to meet Kim Jong Un, the leader of fellow communist country and close ally North Korea. Kim though, arrived in China on his personal train, which he prefers taking to flying.
 When Trump visited Beijing in May, he was greeted by China’s vice president Han Zheng. That move was widely seen by analysts as trading ceremony for substance, as Han’s role is high-level but largely ceremonial.
 When Trump visited in 2017 he was met by China’s top diplomat, as was former US president Obama when he visited in 2014.

 Before and during his visit, protesters demonstrated against the Iran war’s economic impact and the US-led Pax Silica initiative , aimed at securing supply chains for semiconductors, critical minerals and AI.
 Protesters take part in a demonstration against US President Donald Trump's visit to the Philippines for the ASEAN Summit on November 17 in Manila, Philippines. 
 Ezra Acayan/Getty Images 
 Here are some key quotes from the trip: 
 On the South China Sea: Trump said he was “ not concerned at all ” about China’s rising aggression at sea, saying that “it’ll be taken care of” without offering explanation. Vessels from China and the Philippines, a US mutual defense ally, have faced dangerous run-ins in the contested sea.
 On Iran: Trump said the country would pay a major price if it carried out an attack on Washington, after CNN reported that Iran is developing plans to target senior Trump administration officials by detonating a so-called dirty bomb or a chemical weapon in the capital.
 On meeting Kim: Trump said he may also meet with Kim Jong Un if the North Korean leader travels to China. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Trump does not view the potential sit-down as a concession — but stressed no meeting was confirmed.
 On issues back home: Rubio tried to reassure the American public that the recent string of tech outages in the US are unrelated and that no nefarious actors were involved.

 Trump is on his way to China after less than 24 hours in Manila
 By Kevin Liptak in Manila
 President Donald Trump has left the Philippines after a short stop in its capital Manila and is now en route to Shenzhen, China, where he plans to meet with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
 Trump was in Manila for less than a day. He came for a meeting of Southeast Asian leaders, though only caught the tail end of the ASEAN summit. He also met for a lengthy lunch with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. at the Malacañang Palace , which was decked out for Christmas.
 Trump announced new trade measures with Thailand and the Philippines while he was here, but they did not appear to amount to full-blown trade deals.
 US officials hoped Trump’s presence here would demonstrate his commitment to a region where competition with China is fierce.

 No Pax Silica signing, Marcos says, but Philippines to work with US on AI
 By Kathleen Magramo 
 Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr said his government would not be signing an agreement with the United States on the Pax Silica AI supply chain initiative during President Donald Trump’s brief trip to Manila.
 While the Philippines is among 26 signatories the US-led initiative aimed at securing supply chains for semiconductors, critical minerals and AI, exact details on a framework and foreign investment deals have not been announced.
 Asked about details on a signing for a Pax Silica deal, Marcos said: “No…We are not covering that on this trip.”
 Pax Silica has met resistance from environmental and indigenous groups in the Philippines, and sparked protests ahead of Trump’s arrival.

 Who is joining Trump on his Asia trip?
 By Lex Harvey 
 US President Donald Trump is being accompanied by a delegation of top officials and advisers on his trips to the Philippines and China.
 His entourage comprises prominent members of his administration including Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.
 Bessent and Lutnick have clashed recently over restrictions on high-powered AI chips going to China. But Trump said Tuesday the two have handled their disagreement “very well.”
 Also alongside the president is Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, on his first overseas trip since he took over from Susie Wiles last week.
 Natalie Harp, a top aide whose close relationship with the president has sparked headlines , is also in Asia with Trump.
 The world’s richest man, Elon Musk, whose $445 million in political spending failed to deliver Republican majorities in the midterm elections, will be part of the US delegation in Shenzhen.

 Trump touts nuclear energy deal with Philippines, says he's "not concerned" about South China Sea
 By Kathleen Magramo 
 Host TV 
 President Donald Trump touted a potential nuclear energy deal with the Philippines as he sat down with his counterpart Ferdinand Marcos Jr. for a meeting in Manila.
 Trump said the two countries would probably do “something big” on nuclear power. “For the Philippines to embrace American technology in its first modern nuclear project would underscore the strength of the important relationship,” he said.

 Quiet streets and a ban on kites: summit upends daily life for Shenzhen residents
 By CNN staff
 The southern Chinese city of Shenzhen is seen on Wednesday, November 18. 
 Bex Wright/CNN 
 As world leaders descend on the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit this week, life for the tech hub’s 20 million residents will be far from ordinary.
 All roads near the conference venue in the city center are subject to strict traffic controls. And no non-local vehicles are allowed to drive in the city’s six main urban districts.
 Drivers are also being encouraged to switch to public transport. Those who do not drive for four consecutive days are eligible for a 100-yuan ($15) public transport subsidy. As of Monday, nearly 2 million vehicle owners had applied for the scheme. Fares for subways and buses are also cut by half during APEC.
 All roads near the the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit conference venue are subject to strict traffic controls. 
 Bex Wright/CNN 
 Companies have also been encouraged to let their employees work from home to ease commuting pressures. And all primary and junior high schools will be shut from November 17-20 for a fall break.
 “Other than during the Spring Festival, this is the first time I’ve seen traffic so light and roads so clear in downtown Shenzhen,” one user on Douyin, China’s TikTok, wrote, echoing the sentiment of many Shenzhen residents posting on social media.
 The skies will be quieter too — the city has banned drones, kites, balloons and other flying objects from November 11 to 21.
 World leaders descend on the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit this week. 
 Bex Wright/CNN 
 While the roads may be relatively empty, they’ve been beautified with blooms, most of them bougainvillea — Shenzhen’s official flower. Flowers have been installed on over 600 bridges across the city, stretching for a combined length for over 360 kilometers (224 miles), according to a local state-owned outlet .

 Putin said he expects "considerable" benefits from talks with Trump and Xi
 By Lex Harvey 
 Russian President Vladimir Putin arrives at an airport in Shenzhen, China on Wednesday. 
 Kyodo News/Getty Images 
 Russian President Vladimir Putin said Wednesday he expects “considerable potential benefits” from his trilateral meeting with China’s leader Xi Jinping and his US counterpart Donald Trump, Russian state media TASS reported.
 Speaking at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, Putin highlighted a “tectonic shift” in the global economy, with the Asia-Pacific region at its center, TASS reported.
 Putin said the European Union has failed to adapt to the loss of Russian energy, and that Brussels is losing its position, according to TASS. He also touted his country’s economic growth and said Asia-Pacific currently accounts for 53% of Russia’s foreign trade.
 Putin said he expects support for Russia’s bid to chair APEC and host its summit in 2035, TASS reported.
 The Trump-Putin-Xi meeting Thursday — the first ever between the leaders of the three countries — is expected to focus on nuclear non-proliferation, a topic the US president said could yield a new agreement between the world’s biggest nuclear-armed states. Trump has also said he plans to discuss Russia’s war in Ukraine.

 Xi touts China's own "Bay Area," hinting at contest with Silicon Valley
 By Sylvie Zhuang 
 Construction Advances On Guangdong Hong Kong Macao Greater Bay Area Golden Corridor Project on November 5. 
 Shi Jiamin/VCG/AP 
 Chinese leader Xi Jinping hinted that China’s technology is on par with Silicon Valley’s by touting its own Greater Bay Area at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen on Wednesday.
 “Asia-Pacific is home to the world’s most important Bay Area economies, which are characterized by distinct features such as openness, synergy, and spillover effects,” Xi told business executives at the APEC summit, which President Donald Trump will attend.
 Without mentioning the San Francisco Bay Area, home to Silicon Valley, Xi touted China’s own tech capital.
 “Shenzhen, where we are located, is situated within the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau Greater Bay Area.”
 The Greater Bay Area is Beijing’s strategic initiative linking Shenzhen, Hong Kong, Macau, and several other Chinese coastal cities into an integrated economic and high-tech powerhouse.
 Shenzhen has launched tech advances that have put Trump and Xi on a collision course over access to raw materials, advanced chips, and lucrative markets.
 In the tech hub, Xi said, robots work in factories, robot dogs work on farms and drones deliver food.
 “China is a supersized innovation testing ground, where frontier technologies are tested, improved, and upgraded in real-world scenarios, and are then turned into high-quality growth drivers,” he said.
 China supplies the vast majority of the world’s humanoid robots , but has been cut off from its largest export market as the US government moves to curb its reliance on foreign technology.
